utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Once again, let me remind you that you are bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. WITNESS; WITNESS MM-078 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I'll remind you that we're in public session so we won't use names at the moment, but yesterday when we finished you were talking about someone you knew who you described as the last Croat to leave Knin in 1993. And you described how you offered your residence for him to stay in. And you also say that he asked an employee of Mr. Martic to allow him to stay rather than become a refugee. And then I asked you if you knew what Mr. Martic said and your answer was: "I don't know what he told him, but I know he was as sad as I was." I just want to clarify your answer there. When you said: "I know he was as sad as I was," who was as sad as you were in was it the employee of Mr. Martic? Was it Mr. Martic, or was it the Croat that you were speaking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Martic was sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why -- again, without mentioning the name, why was Mr. Martic sad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man was a very close friend of Mr. Martic's and mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. Approximate

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, we were at the end talking about the Dom Kulture centre in Vrpolje, and you told the Trial Chamber yesterday what the function of that place was and you described it, even though you said you didn't like to use the term, you described it as a collection centre for Croats who were leaving the area of Knin. What was -- did the -- did the police in Knin or that area of Knin have any function or responsibility with respect to that place, the Dom Kulture in Vrpolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police in Knin had the responsibility over the Dom Kulture in Vrpolje in terms of protecting the people who were kept in that Dom Kulture from any possible attacks from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the police also facilitate, in any way, the process of Croat civilians going to this location and then leaving the Krajina? Did they organise that in any way or facilitate it in any way to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the police formed part of the logistics team which assisted these people in leaving Knin, that is to say the Republic of Serbian Krajina, smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you know that and if -- if you need to speak about particular people or names, then let me know and we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that because many friends of mine were over there. I can give you their names but in a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go -- Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you know anything about the conditions at this location, at the Dom in Vrpolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions at the Dom were not worthy of human beings. This was a Dom Kulture, which meant that it was a place, a venue, where cultural performances were held. When the people were brought over to the Dom, they were provided from the Red Cross blankets, sort of mattresses, and food in the quantities that were barely enough for them. I have to add that the residents of Knin themselves brought over food as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if the -- that location was ever crowded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area is of a surface of 15 by 20 metres, and it was never overcrowded in terms of the people not being able to have enough space for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long would people typically stay there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the information I have, the longest was three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where would they go when they left there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the convoy went across Lika to Otocac from where it went down to Karlobag. And the last convoy, which was the one in 1993 that my friend left with, it went across Kosovo, Drnis to Zutnic, and then on to Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if the police had any role or function in those convoys that would transport those people from the Dom in Vrpolje to other locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Knin police escorted these buses that formed the convoy to the point where the convoy was taken over by others, where their responsibility ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what point was that? Was that the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The point was at Zitnic, when the convoy went across Drnis. When the convoy went via Otocac then the point was near Gospic. I don't know what the name of the place is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you said that -- you described this last Croat to leave Knin and this last convoy in 1993, are you saying that by 1993, essentially all Croats or virtually all Croats had left the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not all of them left the area. Several Croats remained, but their numbers were insignificant in comparison to the numbers that were there initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say "numbers that were there initially," is that before the conflict began, say 1990 or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I've -- when I was asking you earlier about prisons, you told us that you were aware of a prison at the old hospital in Knin. Did you hear -- did you ever hear about a prison at the fortress in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear about it, but I never had occasion to go to the fortress or the prison, if indeed it was there, and I heard that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about it in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, those are all my questions. Thank you very much. I appreciate your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Nikola Perovic, my co-counsel, will conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I proceed to examine the witness, could I have the usher's assistance in handing out copies of the statement that the witness gave to the OTP in February of last year. There are enough copies for the Trial Chamber, interpreters, and the witness himself. I'd also like us to work in closed session because I will be putting questions to the witness that might put him at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Closed or private?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milena Tanjga is a journalist by professional who worked and lived in Zagreb until 1991. She was the minister for -- of information with Mr. Milan Martic's cabinet. The article was published twice, the latter one was published on the 1st of September, 1995, and the former was published seven days earlier. That is it, if that is enough for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Witness, I have many questions for you. At the beginning of your testimony you said that Mr. Milan Martic was head of a sector in the area of Knin. Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he was the head of sector, not chief, that's the difference. This is the function concerned mostly with the police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphones be enhanced or switched on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may have been a problem of interpretation. I used the word "head," not chief. And if there's a distinction that can be made in the B/C/S, I would appreciate it if it can be made. My question still stands. I beg your pardon, my question is: What sector was this you were saying was head of the police -- this function was concerned mostly with the police. Now, what sector of the police was he head of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the head for one particular area where he was tasked with dealing with the economic crime, political crime, possible disruption of law and order, and the security situation. This particular area covered almost the entire centre of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At that time you, in your position, were you holding a position that was superior to his?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just remind the Court that we're in public session, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. Thank you so much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court is adjourned. Convene tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.04 p.m.,
